What are these funds and what problem are they solving?
Okay, so the problem, we'll start there, is the rising cost of care.
So we actually put out two indices that measure this differently for individuals.
So the first one all site is the Milliman Retiree Healthcare Cost Index.
That measures how much money an individual or a couple will spend over their retirement
lifespan.
So once they retire to when they pass, and the total spend over that period for a mail
with the original Medicare Plus Medigap, which is Plan G plus the Medicare Part D, the drugs,
it's $297,000 for a mail and $340,000 for a female.
So over $600,000 for a couple in retirement.
And that's up on the order of 7% from last year's study and certainly rising over time.
And that's with Medicare, right?
I think that's what a lot of people don't understand is even if you have that backstop,
you still have to have money saved in order to pay for a really basic plan.
So that's in retirement.
The next one is that we put out is called the Milliman Medical Index.
And the Milliman Medical Index measures the cost of providing either an individual just
on a corporate health care plan, so all of your deductibles out of pocket, everything
like that, and then also a typical family of four.
So that number for this year was $37,000 for a family of four is how much one needs just
in a corporate health plan, and $8,460 for an average person.
The rate of inflation in that number that we've been measuring since 2005 is over 6%
per year, so well above someone's typical raise if they're trying to fund this just
out of their salary.
Now how do we try to address this problem with an investment strategy?
So obviously that rate of inflation is well more than tips, is well more than treasuries.
You have to end up taking some risk in order to get to higher returns.
So the way that we do that is there's a third index we publish, and the third index is tracks

So we actually look at claims that we buy data and we get data from providers, so from

that, health care actuaries call that trend.
So the trend in those claims kind of matches what we see in the Milliman Medical Index,
so anywhere from 5% to 6%, it's lately been running well over that, so almost 7%.
In the last 5 years or so.
So the health trend guidelines index, that's what that index is, we use that as our bogey
for the strategy.
So the strategy then seeks to meet that rate of return to try to match that bogey over
time by investing in health care equities, but in health care equities in a specific
way where we identify, I like to call it a follow the money strategy, we try to identify
the companies that benefit when certain trends in inflation are high in health care.
So right now, the trends are high because of drugs, so we're identifying the companies
that are benefiting from the drug costs, and the biggest one right now is Lilly, for example,
and that's our biggest holding in the health care space.
So that's health care equities.
There's also a layer that we call the supply chain, which is broad equities, so that's
all the other things that could cause inflation and a lot of things, so technology gets more
expensive or other things kind of in the broader economy get more expensive, that also pushes
up health care inflation.
Then we have diversifier bucket, and the diversifier that we've chosen serves really two purposes.
So one is to reduce the equity exposure in a drawdown.
So we want something that tends to not be correlated to equities in a drawdown and has
potential to appreciate, and that's gold, but then we also like gold because when paired
with our treasury, which is our de-risking bucket, gold plus treasuries tends to keep
up with wage inflation over time, and then our final bucket is a treasury strategy in
particular that we dial in in order to try to match wage inflation.
So that's how we kind of construct the portfolio to build up to how we seek to meet that level

We're taking things on a weekly basis, everything else on a monthly basis when we get the new

Now, that is based on what has happened roughly five months ago.
So when you submit your claim to your doctor, it takes a while for it to get resolved and

Sometimes there's a back and forth between the insurer and the provider.

So we get essentially what's like a now cast of that health care inflation.
What is it likely trending at right now?
Given that, and then given our model's expected return assumptions for those asset classes,
we assemble the portfolio with the least amount of risk possible in order to meet that objective

And then we do the same thing month over month over month.
And then we also have other features in the equity side that try to help control volatility

So basically we're taking as much risk as we need to, but not more to seek our objective.
